newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Questions remain over Malaysia slowdown - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Questions remain over Malaysia slowdown - analysts.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's admission that a falling ringgit was forcing import cuts confirmed market expectations, but he stopped short of saying how this would be achieved, analysts said on Thursday.
They said Malaysia's plan to cut imports and review setting up of large projects would keep the country's current account deficit in check and prevent overheating in the economy.
"Basically he is saying that the economy's growth will be slowed down. This is what the market wanted," said a regional currency dealer with a large U.S. bank in Singapore.
"Now we have to see how they are going to do it," he added.
Some economists have said that Malaysia, after a decade of eight percent or more growth, was showing signs of strain.

Mahathir said late on Wednesday: "We want to reduce imports because now imports cost a little bit more due to the value of the ringgit has come down. Therefore, for the time being we have to reduce imports."
The Malaysian ringgit has fallen by 11 percent in the last month to around 2.7750 to the dollar on Wednesday due to heavy selling pressure from overseas.
Implementation of some big projects was being reviewed as a "temporary measure" to reduce imports, Mahathir was quoted as telling reporters after meeting a Bosnian delegation.

He said the projects whose implementation was being reviewed were big in value but were not "mega-projects". Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim had said on Tuesday execution of some mega-projects would be postponed.
Mahathir said in reply to a question that the projects would not be postponed but only reviewed to reduce certain imports.
"Now our import cost is a little bit more because the value of ringgit has come down. For the time being, we have got to reduce imports but we will go on with these projects", he said.
The prime minister did not say which projects were under review, which analysts said would be crucial in determining if Malaysia was serious in its attempts to slow down the economy.

"The private sector people build a whole town in Malaysia. You can see they don't build just one or two houses or even one housing scheme. They build a whole town complete with mosques, schools and all that.
"It is nothing, one of them cost about four or five billion ringgit by just one individual. So what is a mega-project?" he said, explaining the concept of mega-project.
"But even if it is done by private sector, we still have to reduce imports," he said.
He once again lashed out against speculators for causing chaos in the country's currency. He also blamed some rich countries for the turmoil in the currency markets.
Mahathir said: "What annoyed me is this kind of activities is actually being supported by very rich countries, and these countries don't even help poor countries."

The prime minister has blamed "rogue speculators" for the chaos in Southeast Asian currencies. He has also named U.S. financier George Soros as mainly responsible for an attack on the region's currencies. Soros has denied any involvement.

"When they see poor countries, they try to knock them on their heads and yet they talk about justice, about democracy -- what democracy is this when the rich can squeeze the poor," he said when asked to comment on the fall of the ringgit.
But, Mahathir said, the Malaysian currency's fall was only temporary and the government was doing its very best towards a "final solution" to the problem.
"We'll recover," he said, but did not elaborate.
